Apple_scab.title: Apple Scab (Fungal Infection)
meds: Apply copper-based fungicides or sulfur sprays early in the season.
For severe infections, use chemical fungicides containing chlorothalonil, myclobutanil, or fenarimol.
care: Prune the tree canopy regularly to increase airflow and sunlight penetration.
Rake and destroy all fallen leaves around the base of the tree to reduce overwintering spores.
prevention: Choose scab-resistant apple cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, Freedom).
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; water at the base of the tree.
Clear wild crabapple trees near your orchard to prevent cross-contamination.

Bacterial_spot.title: Bacterial Spot (Bacterial Infection)
meds: Spray copper-based bactericides (like copper hydroxide) weekly during wet periods.
For early-season protection in stone fruits, streptomycin sprays can be used under agricultural guidance.
care: Never prune or handle plants when foliage is wet, as bacteria spread rapidly in water droplets.
Prune lower branches (bottom 12-18 inches) to prevent bacteria from splashing up from the soil.
prevention: Purchase certified disease-free seeds and transplants.
Use drip irrigation rather than overhead watering to keep foliage dry.
Practice a 2-to-3 year crop rotation, avoiding nightshade crops (tomatoes, peppers, potatoes).

Black_rot.title: Black Rot (Fungal Infection)
meds: Apply copper-based fungicides, captan, or mancozeb starting at bud break.
Organic options include liquid copper sprays or lime-sulfur.
care: Inspect vines regularly and prune out all infected canes, leaves, and mummified berries.
Burn or bury all pruned materials immediately; do not leave them on the ground or in compost.
prevention: Select sunny planting locations with excellent air circulation.
Keep vines properly trained and spaced on trellises to speed up leaf drying.
Control weeds under the vine canopy to reduce humidity.

Cedar_apple_rust.title: Cedar Apple Rust (Fungal Infection)
meds: Apply fungicides containing myclobutanil or copper soap starting at the pink bud stage.
Sulfur sprays can be used as an organic preventive treatment.
care: Remove orange, jelly-like galls from nearby juniper/cedar trees in early spring.
Prune affected apple leaves showing orange rust spots to prevent spread.
prevention: Avoid planting apple trees within a few hundred yards of red cedars or junipers.
Grow rust-resistant apple varieties (e.g., Delicious, Liberty, Winesap).

Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_spot.title: Cercospora / Gray Leaf Spot (Fungal Infection)
meds: Use protective fungicides containing chlorothalonil, copper, or strobilurins when symptoms first appear.
care: Ensure recommended spacing between plants to maximize airflow.
Remove and destroy heavily spotted leaves to limit spore production.
prevention: Rotate crops with non-susceptible plants (e.g., rotate corn/grains with legumes).
Deeply till or plow crop residue after harvest to bury fungal spores in the soil.

Common_rust_.title: Common Rust (Fungal Infection)
meds: Apply sulfur, copper-based fungicides, or neem oil for mild organic control.
Use systemic fungicides (like azoxystrobin) for severe commercial crop infections.
care: Carefully pluck off heavily infected leaves early in the morning.
Water crops at the root level early in the morning so the foliage dries quickly in the sun.
prevention: Grow rust-resistant crop hybrids.
Maintain optimal plant spacing to prevent moisture traps within the canopy.
Destroy weed hosts (like wood sorrel) that act as alternative hosts for rust fungi.

Early_blight.title: Early Blight (Fungal Infection)
meds: Apply copper fungicides or chlorothalonil at the first sign of concentric target-like spots.
Organic gardeners can use Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide.
care: Remove and discard infected lower leaves (do not compost them).
Stake and prune tomato/potato plants to keep foliage off the damp soil.
prevention: Practice a strict 3-year crop rotation for nightshade crops.
Apply a thick layer of mulch (straw or plastic) around the plant base to block soil-borne spores.
Avoid overhead watering; use drip lines or water manually at the base.

Esca_(Black_Measles).title: Esca / Black Measles (Trunk Disease)
meds: There is no direct chemical cure for infected vines.
Use protective pastes or paint containing tebuconazole or copper on pruning cuts to prevent new infections.
care: Postpone pruning until late winter or dry weather when fungal spores are less active.
Prune out diseased wood down to healthy white wood tissue and burn/remove it.
prevention: Always disinfect pruning tools with a 10% bleach solution or isopropyl alcohol between vines.
Seal all pruning wounds larger than 0.5 inches immediately with pruning sealer.

Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).title: Huanglongbing / Citrus Greening (Bacterial Disease)
meds: No chemical cure exists for the disease itself.
Control the Asian Citrus Psyllid vector using systemic insecticides (e.g., imidacloprid) or organic horticultural oils.
care: Provide foliar sprays containing micronutrients (zinc, iron, manganese) to prolong tree productivity.
Aggressively prune and destroy infected limbs, though removing the entire tree is often necessary.
prevention: Buy only certified disease-free citrus stock from licensed nurseries.
Inspect citrus leaves regularly for asymmetrical yellowing and the psyllid insect.
Immediately remove and burn infected trees to protect neighboring citrus groves.

Late_blight.title: Late Blight (Oomycete / Water Mold Infection)
meds: Apply copper-based fungicides or chlorothalonil protectants immediately when regional alerts are active.
Use systemic fungicides like metalaxyl for agricultural control.
care: This is a highly destructive disease. Immediately pull up, bag, and destroy the entire infected plant.
Do not compost infected plants, as spores can survive and spread via wind.
prevention: Plant certified blight-resistant varieties (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant).
Ensure plants are well-spaced and in full sun to dry foliage quickly.
Destroy volunteer tomato/potato plants that emerge in early spring.

Leaf_Mold.title: Leaf Mold (Fungal Infection)
meds: Apply copper fungicides, chlorothalonil, or sulfur-based sprays.
Organic options include potassium bicarbonate sprays.
care: Lower greenhouse/indoor humidity below 85% using fans and ventilation.
Prune lower branches and space plants widely to reduce microclimate humidity.
prevention: Use drip lines instead of overhead sprinklers.
Grow leaf mold-resistant tomato cultivars.
Thoroughly sanitize greenhouse stakes, cages, and structures between seasons.

Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spot).title: Leaf Blight (Fungal Infection)
meds: Spray copper oxychloride or mancozeb at the first sign of symptoms.
Neem oil is a mild organic alternative for early stages.
care: Remove and discard spotted leaves promptly.
Prune internal branches of fruit trees/vines to maximize sunlight penetration.
prevention: Clean up fall leaf debris diligently.
Avoid watering plants late in the evening; ensure leaves do not stay wet overnight.

Leaf_scorch.title: Leaf Scorch (Environmental or Bacterial)
meds: If bacterial (Xylella fastidiosa), there is no chemical cure. Control leafhopper insect vectors with insecticides.
If environmental, apply deep watering and root stimulants instead of chemical meds.
care: Water deeply once or twice a week during dry summer spells rather than shallow daily watering.
Apply a 2-3 inch layer of organic mulch around the root zone to conserve soil moisture.
prevention: Avoid over-fertilizing with high-nitrogen fertilizers, which forces tender growth vulnerable to drying.
Ensure plants are protected from hot, dry wind using windbreaks.
Improve soil drainage in heavy clay soils.

Northern_Leaf_Blight.title: Northern Leaf Blight (Fungal Infection)
meds: Apply foliar fungicides containing propiconazole or azoxystrobin if blight symptoms appear on upper leaves before silking.
care: Promote strong root development through balanced soil nutrition.
Bury crop debris with autumn tillage to accelerate decomposition of fungal spores.
prevention: Plant resistant crop hybrids.
Rotate corn with non-grass crops like soybeans or alfalfa.
Maintain clean borders around fields to reduce alternative grass hosts.

Powdery_mildew.title: Powdery Mildew (Fungal Infection)
meds: Spray potassium bicarbonate, neem oil, sulfur, or copper fungicides.
A home remedy spray of 40% milk and 60% water under sunlight also acts as an effective natural fungicide.
care: Move potted plants to bright, sunny areas, as powdery mildew thrives in cool, shady, humid conditions.
Prune congested center branches to allow air and light to circulate through the plant.
prevention: Water plants early in the morning and from below.
Space plants at recommended distances.
Plant powdery mildew-resistant varieties.

Septoria_leaf_spot.title: Septoria Leaf Spot (Fungal Infection)
meds: Apply copper-based fungicides or chlorothalonil at the first sign of tiny circular spots with grey centers.
care: Stake and cage plants immediately. Prune off all lower branches touching the ground.
Apply mulch to create a barrier between the soil-borne spores and the leaves.
prevention: Practice a 2-year crop rotation away from solanaceous plants.
Thoroughly clean up and discard all plant residues in autumn.
Avoid overhead watering to keep foliage dry.

Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider_mite.title: Spider Mites (Pest Infestation)
meds: Spray with insecticidal soap, neem oil, or horticultural oils.
For severe infestations, use specific miticides (like abamectin) to avoid killing beneficial bugs.
care: Blasts leaves with a strong jet of water from a hose to physically wash mites and webs off.
Mites love dry, dusty environments. Spraying foliage and misting increases humidity, driving them away.
prevention: Release beneficial predatory insects (like ladybugs, lacewings, or Phytoseiidae predatory mites).
Keep plants well-irrigated, as drought-stressed plants are highly vulnerable to mite outbreaks.

Target_Spot.title: Target Spot (Fungal Infection)
meds: Use protective fungicides containing chlorothalonil, copper, or azoxystrobin.
care: Keep plants supported off the ground using stakes or cages.
Prune lower suckers and leaves to increase ventilation.
prevention: Enforce crop rotation.
Irrigate early in the day so leaf moisture evaporates quickly.

Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.title: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl (Viral Infection)
meds: There is no chemical cure for the virus.
Control the silverleaf whitefly vector using insecticidal soaps, neem oil, imidacloprid, or yellow sticky traps.
care: Cover young plants with fine mesh floating row covers to block whiteflies.
Pull up and bag infected plants immediately to prevent whiteflies from carrying the virus to other plants.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties (look for TYLCV-resistant labels).
Eliminate weeds around the garden, as many act as whitefly breeding grounds.
Clean tools after working with infected crops.

Tomato_mosaic_virus.title: Tomato Mosaic (Viral Infection)
meds: There is no chemical treatment or cure.
Wash tools and hands with non-fat dry milk powder or a 20% household bleach solution to deactivate the virus.
care: Remove, bag, and burn/discard the entire plant. Do not compost.
Avoid working with healthy plants immediately after touching diseased ones.
prevention: Use certified disease-free or treated seeds.
Avoid smoking or handling tobacco near tomato plants, as tobacco mosaic virus can cross-contaminate.
Plant resistant varieties.

healthy.title: Healthy Plant Leaf
meds: No medicine needed! The plant is healthy.
care: Provide regular watering at the base of the plant (avoiding wet foliage).
Ensure the plant receives the correct amount of daily sunlight for its species.
Add compost or balanced organic fertilizer according to seasonal guidelines.
prevention: Practice clean gardening by cleaning tools and pots between uses.
Inspect leaves weekly to catch pests or spot signs of leaf discoloration early.
